courses.name: COMP1521 Computer Systems Fundamentals
courses.description: Introduces how computer systems are structured — covering MIPS assembly, integer and floating point representations, file systems, and concurrency.

topics.name: MIPS Basics
topics.description: Introduction to MIPS assembly: registers, basic arithmetic instructions, syscalls, and simple sequential programs.

topics.name: MIPS Control Flow
topics.description: Branching, jumping, labels, and translating C if/else and loops into MIPS assembly.

topics.name: MIPS Functions & Memory
topics.description: Functions, calling conventions, the stack, load/store instructions, arrays in MIPS, and recursion.

topics.name: Integer Representations
topics.description: Binary, hexadecimal, unsigned integers, two's complement signed integers, and integer overflow.

topics.name: Bit Manipulation
topics.description: Bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, NOT), left/right shifts, bit masks, and practical applications.

topics.name: Floating Point Representation
topics.description: IEEE-754 standard, sign/exponent/mantissa breakdown, special values, and floating point precision.

topics.name: File Systems & I/O
topics.description: File system structure, C file I/O system calls, file metadata, directory traversal, and UTF-8 encoding.

topics.name: Concurrency & Processes
topics.description: Processes, fork/exec, process synchronisation with wait(), pthreads, and mutual exclusion.

subtopics.name: MIPS Registers
subtopics.description: The MIPS register file: $t0-$t9 (temporaries), $s0-$s7 (saved), $zero, $v0, $a0-$a3, $ra, $sp.

subtopics.name: Basic Arithmetic Instructions
subtopics.description: li, move, add, sub, addi, mul and simple arithmetic in MIPS.

subtopics.name: Syscalls
subtopics.description: Using syscalls in MIPS: print_int ($v0=1), print_string ($v0=4), read_int ($v0=5), exit ($v0=10).

subtopics.name: Sequential Programs
subtopics.description: Writing complete sequential MIPS programs with .data and .text sections.

subtopics.name: Branch Instructions
subtopics.description: beq, bne, blt, bgt, ble, bge — conditional branching in MIPS.

subtopics.name: Jump Instructions & Labels
subtopics.description: j (unconditional jump), jal (jump and link), jr (jump register), and defining labels.

subtopics.name: If/Else in MIPS
subtopics.description: Translating C if/else statements into MIPS assembly using branches and labels.

subtopics.name: Loops in MIPS
subtopics.description: Translating while and for loops into MIPS assembly.

subtopics.name: Set Less Than (slt)
subtopics.description: slt and slti instructions for comparisons not covered by branch mnemonics.

subtopics.name: Functions with jal/jr
subtopics.description: Calling functions with jal and returning with jr $ra.

subtopics.name: Calling Conventions
subtopics.description: Passing arguments in $a0-$a3 and returning values in $v0-$v1.

subtopics.name: The Stack & Stack Frames
subtopics.description: $sp register, push/pop using addiu $sp and sw/lw, and stack frame layout.

subtopics.name: Load & Store Instructions
subtopics.description: lw, sw (word), lb, sb (byte), lh, sh (halfword) — reading and writing memory.

subtopics.name: Arrays in MIPS
subtopics.description: Accessing array elements using base address + offset: la, lw with offset($reg).

subtopics.name: Recursive Functions
subtopics.description: Implementing recursion in MIPS by saving $ra and arguments on the stack.

subtopics.name: Binary & Hexadecimal
subtopics.description: Binary (base-2) and hexadecimal (base-16) number systems and converting between them.

subtopics.name: Unsigned Integers
subtopics.description: Unsigned integer representation and the range 0 to 2^n - 1 for n-bit values.

subtopics.name: Two's Complement
subtopics.description: Signed integer representation using two's complement: negating, range, and sign extension.

subtopics.name: Integer Overflow
subtopics.description: When overflow occurs in signed and unsigned arithmetic and its consequences.

subtopics.name: Bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT
subtopics.description: The four fundamental bitwise operators: truth tables and behaviour on multi-bit values.

subtopics.name: Bit Shifting
subtopics.description: Left shift (<<) multiplies by powers of 2; right shift (>>) divides; logical vs arithmetic shift.

subtopics.name: Bit Masks & Flags
subtopics.description: Creating masks to test, set, clear, and toggle individual bits or bit fields.

subtopics.name: Applications of Bit Manipulation
subtopics.description: Practical uses: packing data, checking alignment, extracting fields, efficient arithmetic.

subtopics.name: IEEE-754 Standard
subtopics.description: The IEEE-754 floating point standard: single (32-bit) and double (64-bit) precision formats.

subtopics.name: Sign, Exponent & Mantissa
subtopics.description: Breaking a float into 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (biased by 127), and 23 mantissa bits.

subtopics.name: Special Values
subtopics.description: NaN, positive and negative infinity, positive and negative zero in IEEE-754.

subtopics.name: Precision & Rounding Errors
subtopics.description: Why not all real numbers are representable, rounding modes, and accumulation of errors.

subtopics.name: File System Structure
subtopics.description: Inodes, directories, data blocks, and how the OS maps paths to file data.

subtopics.name: File I/O in C
subtopics.description: open(), read(), write(), close(), lseek() — POSIX file descriptor system calls.

subtopics.name: File Metadata & stat()
subtopics.description: File permissions (rwx), size, timestamps, and reading metadata with stat() and lstat().

subtopics.name: Directory Traversal
subtopics.description: opendir(), readdir(), closedir() for iterating directory entries in C.

subtopics.name: UTF-8 Encoding
subtopics.description: How UTF-8 encodes Unicode code points using variable-length 1–4 byte sequences.

subtopics.name: Processes & fork()
subtopics.description: fork() duplicates the calling process; child vs parent via return value; process IDs.

subtopics.name: exec() Family
subtopics.description: execve(), execlp(), execvp() — replacing the process image with a new program.

subtopics.name: Process Synchronisation
subtopics.description: wait() and waitpid() for parent to wait on child exit; zombie and orphan processes.

subtopics.name: Threads with pthreads
subtopics.description: pthread_create(), pthread_join(), thread vs process; shared memory space.

subtopics.name: Mutual Exclusion & Mutexes
subtopics.description: Race conditions, pthread_mutex_lock/unlock, and why locks are needed for shared state.

questions.question: Which of the following registers is used to store the return address when a function is called using the `jal` instruction?
questions.explanation: $ra (return address register) is specifically designated to hold the address of the instruction following a `jal` call, allowing the function to return to the caller.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the $zero register in MIPS?
choices: To always contain the value 0 and cannot be written to
To hold function arguments passed from the caller
To store saved values that must be preserved across function calls
questions.explanation: $zero is hardwired to always read as 0; any write to it is ignored. This makes it useful for operations like clearing a register or implementing logical operations.

questions.question: How many temporary registers ($t0-$t9) are available in the standard MIPS register file?
questions.explanation: The temporary registers range from $t0 to $t9 inclusive, providing exactly 10 temporary registers for use in calculations without preservation requirements.

questions.question: A function receives three integer arguments. Which registers would these arguments be passed in according to the standard MIPS calling convention?
questions.explanation: In MIPS calling conventions, the first four function arguments are passed in registers $a0, $a1, $a2, and $a3; the first three arguments therefore use $a0, $a1, and $a2.

questions.question:
Consider this code fragment:
```
addi $t0, $zero, 5
addi $t1, $zero, 3
add $s0, $t0, $t1
```
What value does $s0 contain after execution?
questions.explanation: $t0 is loaded with 5, $t1 with 3, and then $s0 is assigned the sum of $t0 and $t1, resulting in 8.

questions.question: A function must preserve the value in $s3 across a function call. Which of the following best describes why $s3 is used instead of a temporary register?
choices: $s registers must be saved and restored by the called function, ensuring the caller's value is preserved
$s3 is never used by other functions
Temporary registers cannot hold values larger than 16 bits
questions.explanation: The MIPS calling convention specifies that $s0-$s7 are 'saved' registers; the called function is responsible for saving and restoring them, allowing the caller to rely on their preservation.

questions.question:
A programmer writes the following code intending to set $t0 to 0:
```
addi $t0, $zero, 0
```
Which registers are read from in this instruction?
questions.explanation: The `addi` instruction reads only the first source register ($zero in this case); $t0 is the destination and is written to, not read from.

questions.question: A function receives 6 integer arguments according to MIPS conventions. Where is the 5th argument located?
questions.explanation: Only the first 4 arguments use $a0-$a3; the 5th and subsequent arguments are passed on the stack, typically at offsets from $sp.

questions.question: Consider a scenario where $v0 contains a return value from a function, and immediately afterward the calling code executes `addi $v0, $v0, 1`. What subtle issue might arise if the called function was supposed to return a 32-bit result?
choices: If the result overflows 32 bits after the increment, the overflow is silently ignored in standard MIPS without an exception
$v1 must be used alongside $v0 to hold 64-bit values, but the code only uses $v0
The `addi` instruction cannot operate on return values
questions.explanation: In MIPS, a 64-bit return value uses both $v0 and $v1 together; incrementing only $v0 ignores $v1 and will produce an incorrect result for large values, requiring both registers to be updated together.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction loads the immediate value 100 into register $t0?
questions.explanation: The 'li' (load immediate) pseudo-instruction is the standard way to load a constant value directly into a register. While addi can achieve the same effect, li is the idiomatic choice.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for moving the value in $s0 to $s1?
questions.explanation: The 'move' pseudo-instruction copies the value from the source register ($s0) to the destination register ($s1). MIPS uses 'move' not 'mov', and the destination comes first.

questions.question: Which instruction correctly adds the contents of $t1 and $t2, storing the result in $t0?
questions.explanation: The 'add' instruction takes the destination register first, followed by two source registers in order. The syntax is 'add dest, src1, src2'.

questions.question:
What will be the value in $t0 after these instructions execute?
li $t0, 50
addi $t0, $t0, 25
questions.explanation: The 'li' loads 50 into $t0. The 'addi' (add immediate) then adds 25 to the current value of $t0, resulting in 75.

questions.question:
Trace the following code:
li $s0, 10
li $s1, 3
sub $s2, $s0, $s1
mul $t0, $s2, 2
What is the final value in $t0?
questions.explanation: First, $s0=10 and $s1=3. Then $s2 = 10-3 = 7. Finally, $t0 = 7*2 = 14.

questions.question:
Consider this sequence:
li $t1, -5
addi $t1, $t1, 10
sub $t2, $t1, 3
What is the value in $t2?
questions.explanation: $t1 starts at -5, then -5+10=5. Then $t2=5-3=2. The instruction correctly handles negative immediates and performs subtraction left-to-right.

questions.question:
What is the result of executing this code if $a0 initially contains 0x80000000 (the most negative 32-bit signed integer)?
add $a1, $a0, $a0
questions.explanation: Adding 0x80000000 to itself causes a signed integer overflow in 32-bit MIPS arithmetic. The result wraps around and the overflow flag is set, making the exact result dependent on how the processor handles the exception.

questions.question: Which of these sequences correctly computes $t0 = ($s0 × 4) + 12?
questions.explanation: First multiply $s0 by 4 and store in $t0, then add 12 to $t0. The other options either apply operations in the wrong order or compute incorrect intermediate values.

questions.question:
After executing these instructions, what is in $t3?
li $t0, 100
li $t1, 50
sub $t2, $t0, $t1
mul $t3, $t2, $t2
addi $t3, $t3, -2500
questions.explanation: $t2 = 100-50 = 50. Then $t3 = 50*50 = 2500. Finally, $t3 = 2500 + (-2500) = 0. The sequence carefully sets up a computation that results in zero after the final adjustment.

questions.question: Which syscall number is used to print an integer in MIPS?
questions.explanation: Syscall 1 is the print_int syscall. The integer to be printed must be in $a0 before the syscall is invoked.

questions.question: What must be placed in the $a0 register before calling the print_string syscall?
choices: The memory address of the string to print
The ASCII value of the first character
The string itself (copied into the register)
questions.explanation: The print_string syscall ($v0 = 4) requires the memory address (pointer) of the string in $a0, not the string data itself.

questions.question: Which syscall is used to read an integer from user input?
questions.explanation: Syscall 5 is read_int, which reads an integer from standard input and returns it in $v0.

questions.question:
Consider the following MIPS code:

li $v0, 1
li $a0, 42
syscall

What will be printed to the console?
questions.explanation: This code sets $v0 to 1 (print_int) and $a0 to 42, then calls syscall. The output will be 42.

questions.question: Which register receives the value returned by a read_int syscall?
questions.explanation: The read_int syscall ($v0 = 5) returns the input integer in $v0, from which it must be copied to another register if needed.

questions.question:
Consider this code segment:

li $v0, 4
la $a0, msg
syscall
li $v0, 1
li $a0, 100
syscall

Assuming 'msg' is the label for the string "Number: ", what is the output?
questions.explanation: The first syscall prints the string at address msg ("Number: "), and the second syscall prints the integer 100. The output is the string followed by the number.

questions.question: What is the syscall number for the exit syscall?
questions.explanation: Syscall 10 is the exit syscall, which terminates the program. Optionally, $a0 can contain an exit code.

questions.question:
A programmer writes the following code to print an integer and then exit:

li $v0, 1
li $a0, 7
syscall
li $v0, 10
syscall

What is the potential issue with this code?
choices: The exit syscall should come before print_int
The $a0 register is not preserved between syscalls, so exit will not work correctly
There is no issue; this code is correct
The print_int syscall modifies $v0, so it cannot be reset to 10
questions.explanation: This code is correct. The print_int syscall prints 7, and then the exit syscall terminates the program. Each syscall sets $v0 independently.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code:

li $v0, 5
syscall
move $a0, $v0
li $v0, 1
syscall

Assuming the user inputs 25, what will be displayed?
questions.explanation: The first syscall reads an integer (25) into $v0. The move instruction copies this value to $a0. The second syscall prints the value in $a0, which is 25.

questions.question: In a MIPS program, which section contains variable declarations and data initialization?
questions.explanation: The .data section is used for declaring and initializing variables and global data. The .text section contains executable instructions.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to declare a 32-bit word in the .data section of a MIPS program?
questions.explanation: In MIPS assembly, .word is the directive for declaring 32-bit integers. .int is not standard MIPS syntax; .long and 'w' are incorrect.

questions.question: Which register is typically used as the entry point for a sequential MIPS program execution?
questions.explanation: The program begins execution at the label 'main' in the .text section. While $pc (program counter) tracks execution, 'main' is the named entry point where sequential execution starts.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code segment:
.data
x: .word 10
y: .word 20
.text
main:
  lw $t0, x
  lw $t1, y
  add $t2, $t0, $t1

After execution, what value is in $t2?
choices: Undefined (x and y are not initialized)
questions.explanation: The lw instructions load x (10) into $t0 and y (20) into $t1. The add instruction computes $t0 + $t1 = 10 + 20 = 30, storing the result in $t2.

questions.question: A MIPS sequential program loads a value from memory using 'lw $t0, 0($sp)'. Which of the following best describes what this instruction does?
choices: Loads a word from the address stored in $t0 into memory
Loads a word from the address pointed to by $sp into $t0
Loads a word from $sp offset by 0 bytes into $t0
Stores the word in $t0 to the address in $sp
questions.explanation: The lw instruction loads a word from memory. The operand 0($sp) means the memory address is $sp + 0, and the loaded value goes into $t0. This is correct register-indirect addressing with offset.

questions.question:
In a sequential MIPS program, you declare an array in .data as:
arr: .word 5, 10, 15, 20

What is the memory offset to access the third element (value 15) from the label 'arr'?
questions.explanation: Each .word is 4 bytes. The third element is at index 2 (0-indexed), so offset = 2 × 4 = 8 bytes from the label 'arr'.

questions.question:
A MIPS sequential program contains:
.data
x: .word -5
.text
main:
  lw $t0, x
  add $t1, $t0, $t0
  add $t2, $t1, $t0

What is the final value in $t2, considering two's complement representation?
questions.explanation: x = -5 is loaded into $t0. Then $t1 = $t0 + $t0 = -5 + (-5) = -10. Finally, $t2 = $t1 + $t0 = -10 + (-5) = -15 in two's complement arithmetic.

questions.question: A MIPS program declares multiple variables but a sequential program segment only loads and uses one. After execution, what is guaranteed about the unused variables in memory?
choices: They are automatically freed and their memory is reclaimed
They retain their initialized values exactly as declared in .data
They are overwritten by the program's stack
Their values depend on previous program runs
questions.explanation: In MIPS, variables declared in .data are stored in the static data segment and retain their initialized values throughout program execution unless explicitly modified by load/store instructions. Unused variables are not freed or modified automatically.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS sequential program:
.data
result: .word 0
.text
main:
  li $t0, 7
  li $t1, 3
  sub $t2, $t0, $t1
  sw $t2, result

Assuming 'result' is at memory address 0x10000000, what does the sw instruction do?
choices: Stores the word in result register to address in $t2
Stores the word in $t2 (value 4) to memory address 0x10000000
Stores the word from memory at 0x10000000 to $t2
Stores the word in $t0 minus $t1 to register result
questions.explanation: The sw instruction stores the word in $t2 (which contains 7 - 3 = 4) to the memory address labeled 'result' (0x10000000). The instruction does not use $t2 as an address; it uses $t2 as the source value.

questions.question: What does the MIPS instruction `beq $t0, $t1, label` do?
choices: Branches to label if $t0 is not equal to $t1
Branches to label if $t0 is less than $t1
Branches to label if $t0 is greater than $t1
questions.explanation: beq stands for 'branch if equal'. It compares two registers and branches only when they contain the same value.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction branches when two registers are NOT equal?
questions.explanation: bne stands for 'branch if not equal' and is used to branch when the condition $rs ≠ $rt is true.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for a MIPS branch instruction that branches if $s0 < $s1?
questions.explanation: The correct MIPS syntax for blt (branch if less than) is: blt $rs, $rt, label, where registers are separated by commas and the label comes last.

questions.question:
Trace the following code. If $t0 = 5 and $t1 = 5, which instruction executes immediately after `beq $t0, $t1, skip`?

beq $t0, $t1, skip
addi $t2, $t2, 1
skip: addi $t3, $t3, 2
questions.explanation: Since $t0 equals $t1, the beq condition is true, so the branch is taken to the skip label, executing `addi $t3, $t3, 2` next, skipping the `addi $t2, $t2, 1` instruction.

questions.question:
Trace the following code. If $a0 = 10 and $a1 = 7, what is the final value of $v0?

bgt $a0, $a1, greater
addi $v0, $zero, 0
j end
greater: addi $v0, $zero, 1
end:
questions.explanation: Since $a0 (10) is greater than $a1 (7), the bgt condition is true, so execution branches to 'greater' and $v0 is set to 1.

questions.question:
What will be the result after executing this code if $t0 = 3 and $t1 = 8?

bne $t0, $t1, notequal
addi $t2, $zero, 5
j done
notequal: addi $t2, $zero, 10
done:
questions.explanation: Since $t0 (3) is not equal to $t1 (8), bne branches to 'notequal', setting $t2 to 10 and skipping the instruction that would set it to 5.

questions.question: Consider this code segment with $t0 = -5 (in two's complement). What happens at `blt $t0, $zero, negative`?
choices: The branch is not taken because -5 is represented as a large unsigned number
The branch is taken because -5 is less than 0
The branch is taken because $zero is always larger than any register
The instruction causes an undefined behavior in MIPS
questions.explanation: blt performs a signed comparison. Since -5 (in two's complement) is indeed less than 0, the branch is taken. MIPS correctly interprets negative numbers in signed comparisons.

questions.question: What is the critical difference in behavior between `ble $s0, $s1, label` and `ble $s1, $s0, label`?
choices: They behave identically; the order of operands does not matter
The first branches if $s0 ≤ $s1; the second branches if $s1 ≤ $s0
The first branches if $s0 ≤ $s1; the second branches if $s0 ≥ $s1
MIPS does not support ble with reversed operands
questions.explanation: The ble instruction compares $rs ≤ $rt. In `ble $s0, $s1, label`, it checks $s0 ≤ $s1, but in `ble $s1, $s0, label`, it checks $s1 ≤ $s0, which is equivalent to $s0 ≥ $s1.

questions.question: A programmer writes: `bge $t0, $t1, skip` where $t0 = 0x80000000 (as a 32-bit signed integer, this is -2147483648). If $t1 = 1, will the branch be taken?
choices: Yes, because 0x80000000 is larger when interpreted as unsigned
No, because -2147483648 is less than 1 in signed arithmetic
Yes, because the comparison uses unsigned arithmetic by default
No, because $t1 must be initialized before comparison
questions.explanation: bge performs signed comparison. In signed two's complement arithmetic, 0x80000000 represents -2147483648, which is less than 1, so the branch is NOT taken.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the primary difference between the `j` instruction and the `jal` instruction?
choices: `jal` saves the return address in $ra before jumping, while `j` does not
`j` saves the return address in $ra before jumping, while `jal` does not
`jal` can only jump to labels, while `j` can jump to any address
Both instructions are identical; `jal` is just an alternative mnemonic for `j`
questions.explanation: `jal` (jump and link) is designed for function calls and automatically stores the return address (next instruction's address) in $ra, enabling the function to return. `j` performs an unconditional jump without saving any return address.

questions.question: Which instruction is used to return from a function that was called using `jal`?
questions.explanation: `jr` (jump register) jumps to the address stored in a register. Since `jal` saves the return address in $ra, `jr $ra` is the standard way to return from a function.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the correct syntax for defining a label?
questions.explanation: MIPS labels are defined by placing an identifier followed by a colon (`:`) at the beginning of a line. This label can then be used as the target of jump instructions.

questions.question:
Consider the following MIPS code segment. What value will be in $v0 after execution?
```
jal func
addi $v0, $zero, 5
j end
func: addi $v0, $zero, 10
jr $ra
end: addi $v0, $v0, 3
```
questions.explanation: `jal func` calls the function, setting $v0 to 10 and saving the return address. `jr $ra` returns to the instruction after `jal`, which is `addi $v0, $v0, 3`. This adds 3 to 10, resulting in 13.

questions.question:
Trace through this MIPS code. How many times will the instruction at `loop:` be executed before the program reaches `done:`?
```
addi $t0, $zero, 3
loop: addi $t0, $t0, -1
bne $t0, $zero, loop
done: addi $v0, $zero, 0
```
questions.explanation: $t0 starts at 3. The loop decrements $t0 by 1 each iteration (3→2→1→0). The `bne` branches back while $t0 is not zero, so the loop executes 3 times total before $t0 becomes 0 and the branch fails.

questions.question: What will happen if you execute `jr $zero` in a MIPS program?
choices: The program will jump to address 0, likely causing a crash or undefined behavior
A compile error will be generated
questions.explanation: `jr` jumps to the address stored in the register. Since $zero always contains 0, `jr $zero` attempts to jump to address 0, which is not a valid program address and will cause a runtime error or crash.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code with nested function calls. After `jal func2` completes and control returns to `main`, what is in $ra?
```
main: jal func1
j end
func1: jal func2
jr $ra
func2: addi $v0, $zero, 5
jr $ra
end:
```
choices: The address of the `j end` instruction
The address of the `jal func2` instruction
The address of the `jr $ra` instruction in func1
Undefined; $ra is not modified by nested calls
questions.explanation: When `jal func1` executes, $ra is set to the address of `j end`. When `func1` calls `jal func2`, $ra is overwritten with the return address within func1. After func2 returns, func1 uses `jr $ra` to return to the saved address (`j end`), but $ra now contains func1's return address.

questions.question:
What is the critical issue with this code, and why might it fail?
```
loop: addi $t0, $t0, 1
addi $t1, $t1, 1
j loop
```
choices: The code is syntactically correct but creates an infinite loop with no exit condition
The `j` instruction syntax is incorrect; it should be `j $t0`
Labels cannot be used with `j`; use `jr` instead
The registers $t0 and $t1 are not initialized, causing undefined behavior
questions.explanation: While syntactically valid, this code unconditionally jumps back to `loop` with no branch condition or break mechanism, creating an infinite loop from which the program cannot escape.

questions.question: In a MIPS implementation, when `jal` executes, the return address saved in $ra is the address of which instruction?
choices: The instruction immediately following the `jal` instruction
The label that `jal` is jumping to
The instruction at the end of the called function
questions.explanation: `jal` saves the Program Counter of the next instruction (PC + 4 in a 4-byte instruction architecture) so that when the called function executes `jr $ra`, control returns to the instruction after the `jal` call, not to the `jal` instruction itself.

questions.question: In MIPS, which branch instruction should be used to jump to a label if two registers are NOT equal?
questions.explanation: bne (branch not equal) jumps to the label if the two register values are different. beq branches on equality, and jne is not a valid MIPS instruction.

questions.question: What is the correct structure for translating an if-else statement into MIPS?
choices: Use beq/bne to jump to else label if condition is false, execute if block, then jump over else block to end label
Use beq/bne to jump to if label if condition is true, skip to else, then jump to end
Use only jumps without any labels
Use beq to jump to else only if the condition is true
questions.explanation: The standard pattern branches to the else label when the condition is false, executes the if-block, then jumps to the end to skip the else block. This avoids executing both blocks.

questions.question: In MIPS, what does the label syntax represent in a conditional branch?
choices: A memory address in the code where execution should jump to
A variable that stores a branch condition
A register that holds the branch destination
A comment explaining the branch purpose
questions.explanation: Labels in MIPS represent symbolic names for memory addresses in the code. When a branch instruction is executed, it jumps to the instruction at the labeled address.

questions.question: Consider the C code: if (a > b) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; }. In MIPS, if a and b are in $s0 and $s1 respectively, which instruction should come first after loading the values?
questions.explanation: To check if a > b, we use slt $t0, $s1, $s0 which sets $t0=1 if $s1 < $s0 (i.e., b < a, which means a > b). This sets up the condition for the subsequent branch.

questions.question:
Trace the following MIPS code. Assume $s0 = 5 and $s1 = 3. What is the value of $s2 after execution?
  slt $t0, $s1, $s0
  beq $t0, $zero, else_label
  addi $s2, $zero, 10
  j end_label
else_label:
  addi $s2, $zero, 20
end_label:
questions.explanation: slt sets $t0=1 because 3 < 5. beq does not branch since $t0 ≠ $zero. So the if-block executes, setting $s2=10. The else block is skipped.

questions.question: In translating if (x != 0) in MIPS, which approach correctly checks the condition? Assume x is in $s0.
choices: Use bne $s0, $zero, if_label to jump into the if-block when x is non-zero
Use beq $s0, $zero, if_label to jump into the if-block when x is non-zero
Use slt $t0, $s0, $zero and then beq to check the condition
Use addi to add 1 to $s0 and then jump
questions.explanation: bne (branch not equal) jumps to if_label when $s0 ≠ $zero, which is exactly when x != 0 is true. This directly implements the condition without extra setup.

questions.question:
What is the critical error in the following MIPS if-else translation?
  beq $s0, $s1, else_label
  addi $s2, $zero, 1
else_label:
  addi $s2, $zero, 2
choices: Missing a jump statement to skip the else block after the if block executes
The beq instruction is backwards and should be bne
The labels are not defined properly in memory
The else_label comes after the else block instead of before it
questions.explanation: After executing the if-block (addi $s2, $zero, 1), control falls through to else_label and executes the else block, overwriting $s2. A j end_label is needed after the if-block to skip the else.

questions.question: Consider nested if-else: if (a > 0) { if (b < 10) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; } } else { x = 3; }. How many labels are minimally required for correct MIPS translation?
choices: 4 (labels for: outer else, inner if, inner else, end)
5 (labels for: outer if, outer else, inner if, inner else, end)
questions.explanation: We need: outer_else (jump if a ≤ 0), inner_else (jump if b ≥ 10 inside outer if), end_label (skip remaining code after any branch). The fourth label accounts for the structure of nested conditions.

questions.question: Assume a MIPS if-else translates to: beq $s0, $zero, else_L; addi $s1, $s1, 5; j end_L; else_L: addi $s1, $s1, 10; end_L:. If this runs twice in a loop with $s0 = 5 initially, what is $s1 after two iterations starting from $s1 = 0?
questions.explanation: Each iteration: $s0 = 5 (not zero), so beq doesn't jump. The if-block executes: $s1 += 5. After two iterations: 0 + 5 + 5 = 10. The else block is never executed because $s0 remains 5.

questions.question: In MIPS assembly, which instruction is most commonly used to implement the condition check in a while loop?
questions.explanation: Branch instructions like beq are used to evaluate loop conditions and control whether the loop body executes or the loop exits. Load and store are for memory operations, and add is for arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the label at the beginning of a while loop in MIPS?
choices: To mark where the loop condition is checked so it can be jumped back to
To declare a variable in the loop
To allocate memory for the loop
To increment the loop counter automatically
questions.explanation: Labels mark positions in code that branch instructions can jump to. In loops, the label at the start allows the code to jump back and re-evaluate the condition.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly translates a for loop increment `i++` in MIPS?
questions.explanation: addi (add immediate) with 1 increments a register by 1. subi decrements, beq is a branch, and j jumps unconditionally—none increment properly.

questions.question: Consider this while loop: `while (x < 10) { x++; }` where x is in $t0. After the condition `slt $t1, $t0, 10` is executed, what does $t1 contain if x = 7?
questions.explanation: slt (set less than) sets the destination register to 1 if the first operand is less than the second, and 0 otherwise. Since 7 < 10, $t1 is set to 1.

questions.question:
What is the output of this MIPS loop snippet if $t0 starts at 5?

loop: addi $t0, $t0, -1
bne $t0, $zero, loop
addi $t1, $t1, 1

How many times does the addi $t1, $t1, 1 execute?
questions.explanation: The loop decrements $t0 from 5 to 4, 3, 2, 1, then 0, exiting when $t0 equals zero. This happens 5 times, so addi $t1 executes 5 times.

questions.question: Consider translating `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` into MIPS. Which statement about the loop structure is correct?
choices: The initialization happens before the loop, the condition is checked at the start of each iteration, and the increment happens before the next condition check
The increment happens first, then the condition is checked, then initialization
The condition is checked before initialization
The increment is unnecessary in MIPS
questions.explanation: For loops follow the pattern: initialize once, then repeatedly check condition, execute body, increment, and loop back. This matches standard control flow semantics.

questions.question:
A programmer writes this MIPS code for a while loop but forgets the branch instruction:

loop: lw $t0, 0($sp)
      addi $t0, $t0, 1
      sw $t0, 0($sp)
      # Missing instruction here

Without the missing branch, what happens?
choices: The code executes only once and continues past the loop
The loop executes 10 times by default
questions.explanation: Without a branch instruction (like bne or beq to jump back to the loop label), execution continues sequentially to the next instruction instead of looping, so the loop body executes only once.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS translation of `while (arr[i] != 0) { i++; }` where $t0 = i, $t1 = base address of arr:

loop: sll $t2, $t0, 2
      add $t2, $t1, $t2
      lw $t3, 0($t2)
      beq $t3, $zero, end_loop
      addi $t0, $t0, 1
      j loop
end_loop:

What is the purpose of `sll $t2, $t0, 2`?
choices: To convert the array index to a byte offset (multiply by 4 for word size)
To shift the loop counter left for faster comparison
To allocate space on the stack for the loop
To clear the lower 2 bits of the index
questions.explanation: sll (shift left logical) by 2 multiplies by 4, converting an array index to a byte offset since each word is 4 bytes. This allows proper address calculation for array access.

questions.question: A loop is written as: `for (i = n; i > 0; i--)`. An incorrect MIPS translation uses `slt $t1, $zero, $t0` (instead of `slt $t1, $zero, $t0` after decrement) to check the condition. What goes wrong?
choices: The loop condition is checked before the decrement, causing an off-by-one error where the loop executes one extra time
The loop never executes because slt always returns false
The comparison uses unsigned instead of signed arithmetic
questions.explanation: Placing the condition check before the decrement means the initial condition is tested against the unmodified value. When i=n, the check passes, but the first iteration uses n before decrementing, causing one extra iteration compared to the intended behavior.

questions.question: What does the MIPS instruction `slt $t0, $t1, $t2` do?
choices: Shifts $t1 left by $t2 bits and stores result in $t0
Sets $t0 to the lesser of $t1 and $t2
questions.explanation: The slt instruction performs a signed less-than comparison and sets the destination register to 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. It does not perform a less-than-or-equal comparison, shift operation, or minimum selection.

questions.question: Which instruction would you use to compare a register against an immediate value in MIPS?
questions.explanation: The slti instruction is the immediate variant of slt, allowing comparison with a constant value. The slt instruction requires two registers, and cmp is not a valid MIPS instruction.

questions.question: After executing `slti $t3, $t4, 100`, what value will be in $t3 if $t4 contains 50?
questions.explanation: Since 50 < 100 is true, the slti instruction sets $t3 to 1. The actual values being compared are not stored in the destination register; only the boolean result (1 for true) is stored.

questions.question:
Consider this code snippet:
```
addi $t1, $zero, 10
addi $t2, $zero, -5
slt $t0, $t1, $t2
```
What value will be in $t0 after execution?
questions.explanation: The slt instruction compares $t1 (10) with $t2 (-5). Since 10 is not less than -5, the condition is false and $t0 is set to 0. The slt instruction performs signed comparison, so -5 is correctly interpreted as negative.

questions.question: Which of the following code sequences correctly uses slt to implement the conditional branch `if (x < y) goto label`?
questions.explanation: To implement `if (x < y)`, we use slt to compare $s0 (x) and $s1 (y), storing the result in $t0. If the result is 1 (true), we branch. The second option reverses the comparison, and the third uses an immediate with a non-sensical value.

questions.question:
After executing this sequence:
```
addi $t1, $zero, -32768
addi $t2, $zero, -32769
slti $t0, $t1, -32769
```
What is in $t0?
questions.explanation: The slti instruction compares $t1 (-32768) with the immediate value -32769. Since -32768 is greater than -32769, the condition is false and $t0 is set to 0. Both values are within the valid signed 16-bit range for the immediate.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the key difference between slt and sltu instructions?
choices: slt works with registers while sltu only works with immediates
slt performs signed comparison while sltu performs unsigned comparison
slt sets the register to the smaller value while sltu sets it to 1 or 0
slt uses two operands while sltu uses three operands
questions.explanation: The slt instruction interprets operands as signed integers, while sltu interprets them as unsigned integers. This affects how negative values are treated in the comparison. Both instructions set the destination to 1 or 0 based on the comparison result.

questions.question: Consider the instruction `slti $t0, $t1, 32767`. What problem might occur if you try to use `slti $t0, $t1, 32768`?
choices: The instruction will cause a segmentation fault
The immediate value 32768 exceeds the 16-bit signed range and cannot be directly represented in the instruction
$t1 will be overwritten with an incorrect value
questions.explanation: The immediate field in slti is limited to 16 bits and interprets values as signed (-32768 to 32767). The value 32768 cannot fit in this range. The assembler would either reject this or implicitly load the value into a register using a pseudo-instruction.

questions.question:
What would be the result of this code sequence?
```
addi $t1, $zero, -1
slt $t0, $t1, $zero
sltu $t2, $t1, $zero
```
questions.explanation: For slt: -1 (signed) < 0 is true, so $t0 = 1. For sltu: -1 is interpreted as 4294967295 (unsigned 32-bit), which is not less than 0, so $t2 = 0. The difference in signed vs. unsigned interpretation is the key distinction.

questions.question: In MIPS, which instruction is used to call a function and automatically save the return address?
questions.explanation: jal (jump and link) both jumps to the function address and saves the return address in $ra (register 31). The other instructions either jump without saving (j), return from a function (jr), or are conditional branches (beq).

questions.question: What is the correct instruction to return from a function to the caller in MIPS?
questions.explanation: jr $ra (jump register) performs an indirect jump to the address stored in $ra, which is the return address saved by jal. The 'r' in jr indicates it uses a register value, not an immediate address.

questions.question: In MIPS, register $ra is automatically set by which instruction?
questions.explanation: The jal instruction automatically loads the return address (address of the next instruction after jal) into $ra. No other instruction shown performs this automatic assignment.

questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:

```
main:
  jal add_numbers
  # line X
  
add_numbers:
  add $v0, $a0, $a1
  jr $ra
```

What address does $ra contain when add_numbers executes jr $ra?
choices: The address of the jal instruction
The address of line X (the instruction after jal)
The address of the add instruction inside add_numbers
The address of the jr $ra instruction
questions.explanation: jal saves the address of the next instruction (the one after jal) into $ra. This allows the function to return to the correct location in the calling code when jr $ra executes.

questions.question:
Trace the execution of this MIPS code:

```
  li $a0, 5
  jal double
  move $a0, $v0  # line A
  
double:
  add $v0, $a0, $a0
  jr $ra
```

What value is in $a0 after the jr $ra instruction returns?
questions.explanation: jal double causes $ra to be set to the address of 'line A'. The double function sets $v0 to 10 (5+5), then jr $ra returns to line A, which moves $v0 (10) into $a0.

questions.question: If a function modifies $ra during execution but needs to call another function via jal, what must the function do?
choices: Nothing, $ra is automatically preserved by the CPU
Save $ra to the stack before calling jal, then restore it before returning
Use j instead of jal for nested calls
Copy $ra to another register like $s0 before the second jal
questions.explanation: Since jal overwrites $ra with a new return address, a function that needs to make nested function calls must save $ra to the stack before the nested jal, then restore it before executing its own jr $ra to ensure it returns to its caller.

questions.question:
Consider this buggy MIPS code:

```
func:
  add $v0, $a0, $a1
  jal another_func
  jr $ra
  
another_func:
  sub $v0, $v0, 1
  jr $ra
```

Why will this code not work correctly?
choices: The jr $ra in func will jump to the wrong address because jal overwrote $ra
The sub instruction will corrupt the return value
The jal instruction must use a label, not an address
The add and sub instructions cannot both modify $v0
questions.explanation: When jal another_func executes, it overwrites $ra with the return address pointing to jr $ra in func. However, func then immediately executes jr $ra, jumping to the middle of func instead of returning to the caller. func should save $ra before calling another_func.

questions.question: In a MIPS function, if you need to preserve the value in $ra across multiple function calls, which approach is correct?
choices: Copy $ra to $s0 before each jal, then copy it back
Use the stack to push $ra before nested jals, and pop it before the final jr $ra
Avoid using jal and use j with manual address calculations instead
Declare a global variable to store $ra
questions.explanation: The standard convention is to save $ra (and other caller-saved registers) to the stack upon function entry if the function makes nested calls, then restore before returning. This is the only reliable, convention-following approach.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the jal instruction and the $31 register in MIPS?
choices: $31 is an alias for $ra; jal saves the return address to $31
jal uses $31 internally but the programmer should always use $ra
$ra and $31 are different registers; jal stores to $ra only
jal stores to $31, and $ra is a separate register that must be manually updated
questions.explanation: $31 and $ra are the same register—$ra is the conventional name for register 31. When jal executes, it saves the return address into this register, regardless of whether you refer to it as $ra or $31.

questions.question: In MIPS calling conventions, which registers are used to pass the first four integer arguments to a function?
questions.explanation: $a0-$a3 are the argument registers designated by the MIPS calling convention for passing integer arguments. The other registers serve different purposes: $v0-$v1 are for return values, $s0-$s3 are saved registers, and $t0-$t3 are temporary registers.

questions.question: In MIPS, where should a function place its return value(s)?
choices: $v0 for a single value, or $v0-$v1 for two values
questions.explanation: The MIPS calling convention specifies that return values go into $v0 (for a single 32-bit value) or $v0-$v1 (for two 32-bit values). The other registers are used for arguments, stack management, and control flow respectively.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly shows how to pass three arguments (10, 20, 30) to a function in MIPS?
questions.explanation: Arguments are passed in $a0, $a1, $a2 (and $a3 for a fourth argument). Using li to load immediate values into these registers is the correct way to prepare arguments before a function call.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code:
```
li $a0, 5
li $a1, 3
jal multiply
move $s0, $v0
```
Assuming `multiply` returns the product in $v0, what will be stored in $s0 after execution?
questions.explanation: The function `multiply` is called with arguments 5 and 3 in $a0 and $a1 respectively. It should return their product (15) in $v0, which is then moved into $s0. This traces through the calling convention correctly.

questions.question: A function receives four arguments in $a0-$a3. If the function needs to preserve one of these argument values after making a call to another function, what should it do?
choices: Save the argument value to the stack before calling the other function
Move it to a $t register before calling
Call the other function with fewer arguments to avoid overwriting
questions.explanation: Argument registers $a0-$a3 are not preserved across function calls and will be overwritten. To preserve a value, it must be saved to the stack or moved to a saved register like $s0-$s7 before making a nested call.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following MIPS code?
```
li $a0, 100
jal addTen
add $v0, $v0, $a0
```
Assuming `addTen` takes the value in $a0, adds 10 to it, and returns the result in $v0?
questions.explanation: After `jal addTen`, $v0 contains 110 (100 + 10), but $a0 still holds 100 (argument registers are not preserved by the callee). The add instruction then computes 110 + 100 = 210 and stores it in $v0.

questions.question: A function takes two arguments in $a0 and $a1, performs calculations, and needs to return two different results. Where should these results be placed?
questions.explanation: The MIPS calling convention allows functions to return two 32-bit values using $v0 and $v1. Reusing $a0 or $a1 would overwrite the input arguments, and $s registers are caller-saved so inappropriate for return values.

questions.question:
Consider a nested function call where `main` calls `funcA`, which then calls `funcB`. `funcA` needs to preserve the value in $a0 before calling `funcB` because `funcB` will overwrite it. Which of the following approaches is correct?
```
A) Save $a0 to stack before jal funcB, restore after
B) Copy $a0 to $s3 before jal funcB
C) Move $a0 to $t0 before jal funcB
D) Move $a0 to $v0 before jal funcB
```
choices: Both A and B are correct
questions.explanation: Both approaches work: saving to the stack (A) is always safe, and saving to a saved register like $s3 (B) is also valid since $s registers are caller-saved and $funcB must preserve them. Temporary registers ($t0) and return registers ($v0) are not guaranteed to be preserved across calls.

questions.question: A function receives arguments in $a0, $a1, $a2, and $a3. It calls another function that also takes 4 arguments. After the inner function call completes, the outer function tries to use $a2 but finds it has been changed. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The inner function overwrote $a2 as it loaded its own arguments, because $a0-$a3 are not preserved by the callee
The stack pointer moved and corrupted the data
The outer function forgot to use jal instead of j
The return address in $ra was not saved properly
questions.explanation: Argument registers $a0-$a3 are not preserved by the callee according to MIPS calling convention. When the inner function loads its own arguments into $a0-$a3, it overwrites whatever the outer function had stored there. The outer function must save values it needs to preserve before making a nested call.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the primary purpose of the $sp (stack pointer) register?
choices: To store the memory address of the top of the stack
To hold the return address of the current function
To store the base address of the data segment
To indicate the number of items currently on the stack
questions.explanation: $sp always points to the current top of the stack. It is decremented when pushing values (allocating space) and incremented when popping values (deallocating space).

questions.question: Which instruction correctly pushes a 32-bit word onto the stack in MIPS?
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is to first decrement $sp by 4 (allocate space), then write the value to the memory location now pointed to by $sp.

questions.question: In a MIPS stack frame, what does the frame pointer ($fp) typically point to?
choices: The address of the saved return address on the stack
The top of the stack (same as $sp)
The first local variable of the current function
The base address of the current function's code segment
questions.explanation: $fp is typically set to point to the saved $ra (return address) on the stack, providing a stable reference point for accessing local variables and arguments that may be stored at fixed offsets from this location.

questions.question:
Consider the following MIPS code executed at the start of a function. What is the net change to $sp after both instructions execute?

addiu $sp, $sp, -8
addiu $sp, $sp, -4
questions.explanation: The first instruction decreases $sp by 8, and the second decreases it by 4. The total change is -8 + (-4) = -12, so $sp decreases by 12.

questions.question:
A function allocates 16 bytes on the stack for local variables and then saves $s0 at offset 0 (relative to $sp after allocation). Which instruction correctly saves $s0?

Assume $sp has already been decremented by 16.
questions.explanation: After $sp is decremented by 16, $sp already points to the top of the allocated frame. Offset 0 from $sp accesses the first word of the newly allocated space, which is the correct location for saving $s0.

questions.question: A function prologue saves two registers ($ra and $s0) on the stack in order, then allocates space for 2 local variables (8 bytes total). After $sp is decremented by 16, what is the stack offset of $ra from the current $sp?
questions.explanation: $ra is saved first at offset 0, then $s0 is saved at offset 4. Local variables occupy offsets 8-15. From the current $sp, $ra is at offset 8 (2 words up the stack).

questions.question:
A programmer writes the following stack manipulation code:

addiu $sp, $sp, -4
sw $t0, 0($sp)
lw $t1, 0($sp)
addiu $sp, $sp, 4

What is the relationship between $t0 and $t1 after this code executes, assuming no other code modifies memory?
choices: $t1 contains the same value that was in $t0
questions.explanation: $t0 is pushed onto the stack, then immediately popped into $t1 at the same memory location. Since no other code modified that memory, $t1 receives the exact value that was in $t0.

questions.question: A function correctly allocates 24 bytes for its stack frame (including saved registers and local variables). The function then calls a nested function, which allocates an additional 16 bytes. After the nested function returns and $sp is restored, but before the outer function deallocates its frame, what should $sp point to?
choices: 24 bytes below the original $sp at function entry
40 bytes below the original $sp at function entry
16 bytes below the original $sp at function entry
The same value as the original $sp at function entry
questions.explanation: Each function must restore $sp to point to its own stack frame before returning. The nested function's 16-byte allocation is deallocated when it returns, leaving only the outer function's 24-byte allocation.

questions.question: A function prologue does: `addiu $sp, $sp, -20`. Later, the code attempts to restore a saved register with: `lw $s0, 20($sp)`. Which of the following is true?
choices: The register is loaded from memory 20 bytes above the current $sp, which is outside the allocated frame and likely incorrect
The register is correctly restored because the offset accounts for the 20-byte allocation
The instruction is a syntax error in MIPS
The register is loaded from the top of the stack, which is always correct
questions.explanation: After `addiu $sp, $sp, -20`, the allocated frame extends from current $sp to 20 bytes above it. Loading from offset 20($sp) accesses memory 20 bytes above the current $sp, which is outside the frame. Saved registers should be within the frame, typically at lower offsets like 0, 4, 8, etc.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction loads a 32-bit word from memory into a register?
questions.explanation: lw (load word) loads a full 32-bit word from memory. lb loads a byte, lh loads a halfword, and sw stores a word.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for storing a byte to memory at address in $s0?
questions.explanation: sb (store byte) is used to write an 8-bit byte to memory. sh stores a halfword, sw stores a word, and lb loads a byte.

questions.question: Which instruction loads a 16-bit halfword from memory?
questions.explanation: lh (load halfword) loads a 16-bit value from memory into a register. lw loads 32 bits, lb loads 8 bits, and sh stores rather than loads.

questions.question: Consider this code: lw $t0, 4($sp) followed by sw $t0, 8($sp). If $sp contains 100 and the word at address 104 is 42, what is stored at address 108?
questions.explanation: lw loads the word from address 104 (100+4) which contains 42 into $t0. sw then stores that value (42) to address 108 (100+8).

questions.question: Given memory at address 0x1000 contains 0xAABBCCDD. After executing lb $t0, 0($s0) where $s0 = 0x1000, what is in $t0?
questions.explanation: lb loads the least significant byte (rightmost) from memory, which is 0xDD. The loaded byte is zero-extended into the 32-bit register.

questions.question: After executing lh $t2, 2($t1) where $t1 = 0x2000 and memory at 0x2002 contains 0x5678, what does $t2 contain?
questions.explanation: lh loads a 16-bit halfword from address 0x2002 (0x2000+2), which is 0x5678. The value is zero-extended into the 32-bit register as 0x00005678.

questions.question: Consider this code sequence: sw $t0, 0($sp); lw $t1, 0($sp); lb $t2, 0($sp). If $t0 initially contains 0xAABBCCDD, what value is loaded into $t2?
questions.explanation: sw stores the full 32-bit word 0xAABBCCDD to memory. lb loads only the byte at that address (the least significant byte 0xDD), zero-extending it to 0x000000DD.

questions.question: A program stores multiple halfwords: sh $t0, 0($s0); sh $t1, 2($s0). If $t0 = 0x1111 and $t1 = 0x2222, what 32-bit word is now at address $s0?
questions.explanation: sh stores $t0 (0x1111) at offset 0 and $t1 (0x2222) at offset 2. In little-endian MIPS, the word at $s0 is 0x22221111 (higher offset stores to higher address bits).

questions.question: Given lw $t0, -4($fp) where $fp = 0x3000, followed by sb $t0, 100($sp) where $sp = 0x2000, and $t0 contains 0x12345678, what byte is written to memory?
questions.explanation: sb stores only the least significant byte of $t0 (0x78) to address 0x2064 (0x2000+100). The other bytes are ignored in a byte store operation.

questions.question: In MIPS, what does the `la` instruction do when used with an array?
choices: Loads the base address of the array into a register
Loads the first element of the array into a register
Loads a single byte from the array address
Loads and adds the array offset to the current address
questions.explanation: The `la` (load address) instruction loads the base memory address of an array into a register, which is then used as a base for subsequent element access with offsets.

questions.question: If an integer array starts at address 0x10000000 in memory, what is the correct MIPS syntax to load the element at index 2 into $t0?
questions.explanation: Array index 2 with 4-byte integers requires an offset of 2 × 4 = 8 bytes from the base address; `lw` uses byte offset, not element index.

questions.question: Which register typically holds the base address of an array in MIPS function calls?
questions.explanation: By MIPS calling convention, the first argument to a function (often an array address) is passed in $a0, making it the natural choice for the base address.

questions.question: Consider this MIPS code: `la $s0, array` followed by `lw $t1, 12($s0)`. If array contains integers [5, 10, 15, 20, 25], what value is loaded into $t1?
questions.explanation: Offset 12 bytes with 4-byte integers = index 3 (12 ÷ 4 = 3), so element array[3] = 20 is loaded.

questions.question: A programmer writes code to access array[i] where i is stored in $t2. Which instruction sequence correctly loads array[i] into $t0?
questions.explanation: The offset must be computed: multiply index by 4 (left shift by 2), add to base address, then use that in lw with offset 0; lw does not support register offsets directly.

questions.question: Trace this code: `la $a0, arr` (arr at 0x1000), `lw $t0, 0($a0)`, `lw $t1, 4($a0)`, `lw $t2, 8($a0)` where arr = [100, 200, 300]. What are the values in $t0, $t1, $t2?
questions.explanation: Each `lw` with different offsets (0, 4, 8 bytes) loads consecutive 4-byte integers from the array in order: 100, 200, 300.

questions.question: Consider an array of bytes (not words). To access byte at index i in array, what offset should be used in `lb $t0, offset($s0)` where $s0 is the base address?
questions.explanation: For byte arrays, each element is 1 byte, so the offset is just the index i; multiplication by 4 is only needed for word (32-bit) arrays.

questions.question: A programmer mistakenly uses `lw $t0, 5($s0)` to access array[1] in a word array. What is the most likely error?
choices: Offset 5 is not a multiple of 4, causing unaligned memory access or incorrect data
The la instruction was not used before lw
$s0 does not contain the correct base address
questions.explanation: Word (32-bit) arrays require offsets in multiples of 4; offset 5 is unaligned and will either cause an exception or load from an incorrect address, mixing bytes from adjacent words.

questions.question: Given a 2D array in row-major order: `int arr[3][4]` starting at address $s0, what is the correct offset to access arr[1][2]?
questions.explanation: In row-major order with 4 columns, element [1][2] is at linear position (1×4 + 2) = 6; multiplying by 4 bytes per integer gives offset 24.

questions.question: In MIPS, which register must be saved on the stack before making a recursive function call to preserve the return address?
questions.explanation: $ra (return address) contains the address where the function should return, and it gets overwritten when a new function is called, so it must be saved on the stack in recursive functions.

questions.question: What is the primary reason for saving function arguments on the stack in a recursive MIPS function?
choices: To comply with the MIPS calling convention when $a0-$a3 need to be reused in recursive calls
Because registers run out of space and the stack is unlimited
To make the code execute faster
To prevent integer overflow in arithmetic operations
questions.explanation: Recursive calls reuse the argument registers $a0-$a3, so previous values must be saved to the stack to preserve the caller's arguments across the recursive call.

questions.question: In a MIPS recursive function, what is the typical first instruction after the function label?
questions.explanation: The function must allocate stack space (by decrementing $sp) before saving registers and local variables, which is done with addiu $sp, $sp, -size.

questions.question: Consider a recursive factorial function where $a0 holds the input n. After saving $ra and $a0 on the stack, making a recursive call with jal factorial, and then loading them back, which order must the loads occur?
choices: Load $a0 first, then $ra (reverse order of saves)
Load $ra first, then $a0 (same order as saves)
Order doesn't matter as long as addresses are correct
questions.explanation: Saved values must be loaded in reverse order (LIFO) from a stack; if $a0 was saved first (deeper on stack) and $ra second (closer to sp), $ra must be loaded first, then $a0.

questions.question:
Trace through this MIPS code snippet for a recursive call:
```
addiu $sp, $sp, -8
sw $ra, 4($sp)
sw $a0, 0($sp)
jal recursive_func
lw $a0, 0($sp)
lw $ra, 4($sp)
```
After the `jal` instruction executes, what value is now in $ra?
choices: The return address of the current (recursive) function call
The return address of the previous function call (unchanged)
The address of the instruction immediately after jal
questions.explanation: The `jal` instruction overwrites $ra with the return address of the recursive call; the old $ra was saved to the stack at offset 4($sp) before this happened.

questions.question:
A recursive MIPS function saves $ra and $a0-$a2 on the stack using these instructions:
```
addiu $sp, $sp, -16
sw $ra, 12($sp)
sw $a0, 8($sp)
sw $a1, 4($sp)
sw $a2, 0($sp)
```
When restoring before returning, which instruction correctly restores $ra?
questions.explanation: $ra was saved at offset 12($sp), so it must be restored from the same address; the offset must match exactly where it was stored.

questions.question: A recursive function calls itself twice: once with `jal func` and then later makes another `jal func` call. Before the second `jal`, the programmer failed to restore $ra from the stack between the two calls. What will happen?
choices: The first recursive call will return to the wrong address, causing incorrect control flow
Both recursive calls will execute correctly because $ra is updated each time
The program will crash immediately with a segmentation fault
The second jal will overwrite $ra again, so the first call's return address is still accessible on the stack
questions.explanation: When the first recursive function returns via `jr $ra`, it will jump to the return address of the second `jal` instead of the correct return address of the first call, since $ra was overwritten and never restored.

questions.question: Consider this recursive Fibonacci implementation where stack space is allocated as `addiu $sp, $sp, -12`. The function saves $ra, $a0, and $v0. After calling the function recursively twice with different arguments, if the second recursive call's $ra restore instruction is placed at offset 8($sp) instead of 4($sp), what is the consequence?
choices: $ra will be restored from the saved $a0 value, causing a jump to an invalid memory address
The function will still work correctly because the CPU automatically detects the error
Only the first recursive branch will be affected, not the second
$sp will be corrupted and cause a stack overflow
questions.explanation: Restoring from the wrong offset means $ra will load whatever value was stored at that address; if $a0 was saved there, $ra will contain $a0's value, causing an invalid return address.

questions.question: A recursive function uses `addiu $sp, $sp, -16` to allocate stack space but only saves and restores $ra (8 bytes allocated for it) and one other register. Before returning, the programmer uses `addiu $sp, $sp, 12` instead of 16 to deallocate. What is the side effect?
choices: $sp will point 4 bytes above where it should, leaving 4 bytes of unused allocated stack space permanently
The return address will be corrupted because $sp doesn't align to its original value
The next function call will overwrite the leftover 4 bytes, causing data loss
No error will occur because MIPS doesn't enforce stack pointer consistency
questions.explanation: Deallocating fewer bytes than allocated leaves the stack pointer misaligned relative to the function's prologue; the 4-byte gap remains and the stack frame contract is broken for subsequent functions.

questions.question: What is the hexadecimal equivalent of the binary number 1010 1100?
questions.explanation: Binary 1010 converts to hex A (10) and 1100 converts to hex C (12), giving AC. Each group of 4 binary digits maps directly to one hexadecimal digit.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid hexadecimal number?
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F only. 0x1A2F contains only valid hex characters (1, A, 2, F). The other options contain G, which is not a valid hexadecimal digit.

questions.question: Convert the binary number 11111111 to decimal. What is its hexadecimal representation?
questions.explanation: Binary 11111111 equals decimal 255. In hexadecimal, each F represents 15, so FF represents 15×16 + 15 = 255, written as 0xFF.

questions.question: What is the binary representation of hexadecimal 0x3D?
questions.explanation: Hex 3 = binary 0011 and hex D (13) = binary 1101. Concatenating these gives 0011 1101.

questions.question: You need to store the value 4095 in a variable. How many hexadecimal digits are required to represent this number without leading zeros?
questions.explanation: 4095 in hexadecimal is 0xFFF (15×256 + 15×16 + 15 = 4095). This requires exactly 3 hex digits. 0xFF (2 digits) can only represent up to 255.

questions.question: A MIPS instruction loads the value 0xDEADBEEF into register $t0 using li $t0, 0xDEADBEEF. In binary, what are the last 8 bits of this value?
questions.explanation: 0xEF in hexadecimal converts to binary 1110 1111. The last 8 bits come from the rightmost hex byte EF, which is 1110 1111.

questions.question: Which binary number, when converted to hexadecimal, produces 0x80?
questions.explanation: 0x80 = 8 in the first hex digit (binary 1000) and 0 in the second (binary 0000), giving 1000 0000. This equals decimal 128.

questions.question: Consider converting 0x1FF to binary, then interpreting only the lowest 8 bits as a separate binary number. What is this 8-bit value in hexadecimal?
questions.explanation: 0x1FF in binary is 0001 1111 1111. The lowest 8 bits are 1111 1111, which equals 0xFF in hexadecimal. This demonstrates masking with 0xFF to extract the lower byte.

questions.question: A programmer attempts to convert 0xAB5 to binary by converting each hex digit separately: A→1010, B→1011, 5→0101. What is the resulting binary representation, and is this approach correct?
choices: 1010 1011 101; incorrect, missing a leading zero in the last group
101 1011 1010; correct but digits in reverse order
questions.explanation: Converting each hexadecimal digit individually to 4-bit binary is the correct approach: A=1010, B=1011, 5=0101, giving 1010 1011 0101. This is a standard and reliable conversion method.

questions.question: For an unsigned integer represented with 8 bits, what is the maximum value that can be represented?
questions.explanation: An 8-bit unsigned integer can represent values from 0 to 2^8 - 1 = 255. This is the maximum value before overflow occurs.

questions.question: How many distinct values can be represented using a 16-bit unsigned integer?
questions.explanation: A 16-bit unsigned integer can represent 2^16 = 65536 distinct values (from 0 to 65535 inclusive).

questions.question: What is the minimum value in the range of a 32-bit unsigned integer?
questions.explanation: Unsigned integers have no negative values; the minimum representable value is always 0 for any bit width.

questions.question: A 4-bit unsigned integer is incremented from its maximum value. What happens?
choices: It stays at the maximum value
questions.explanation: The maximum 4-bit unsigned value is 15 (2^4 - 1). Incrementing 15 by 1 causes overflow, and the value wraps around to 0 due to modular arithmetic.

questions.question: If you store the decimal value 300 in an unsigned 8-bit integer in C, what value is actually stored?
questions.explanation: 300 exceeds the maximum 8-bit unsigned value of 255. The stored value is 300 mod 256 = 44, because only the lower 8 bits are retained.

questions.question: In MIPS, if register $t0 contains the maximum value for a 32-bit unsigned integer and you execute 'addu $t0, $t0, 1', what is the result in $t0?
questions.explanation: The 'addu' (add unsigned) instruction performs modular arithmetic. Adding 1 to 2^32 - 1 wraps around to 0 due to 32-bit overflow.

questions.question: Consider a system where an unsigned integer is represented with n bits. After performing multiple arithmetic operations, a value exceeds 2^n - 1. Which statement is most accurate about the stored result?
choices: The value is truncated to fit within n bits using modular arithmetic
The system automatically expands to use more bits
A runtime error occurs and the program crashes
The excess bits are stored in a separate overflow register
questions.explanation: Unsigned integer overflow is handled through modular arithmetic; only the lower n bits of the result are stored, effectively computing the value modulo 2^n.

questions.question: A program uses unsigned 16-bit integers. Two values are added: 40000 + 30000. What is the resulting value stored in the 16-bit unsigned integer, and what mathematical operation explains this?
choices: 30000, because the first operand is discarded
questions.explanation: 40000 + 30000 = 70000, which exceeds 65535 (2^16 - 1). The result wraps using modulo: 70000 mod 65536 = 4464.

questions.question: In a hypothetical 6-bit unsigned system, what is the range of representable values, and how many distinct values can be represented?
questions.explanation: A 6-bit unsigned integer represents 2^6 = 64 distinct values in the range [0, 2^6 - 1] = [0, 63].

questions.question: In two's complement representation, how do you negate a signed integer?
questions.explanation: Two's complement negation is performed by inverting all bits (one's complement) and then adding 1 to the result. This is the standard algorithm for negating signed integers in two's complement.

questions.question: What is the range of values that can be represented using 8-bit two's complement signed integers?
questions.explanation: For n-bit two's complement, the range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For 8 bits: -2^7 to 2^7 - 1 = -128 to 127.

questions.question: In 16-bit two's complement, what is the bit pattern for the value -1?
questions.explanation: In two's complement, -1 is represented as all 1 bits. This is because flipping all bits of 0 (00...00) gives all 1s, and adding 1 results in overflow back to all 1s.

questions.question: You have a 32-bit signed integer with the value 0x7FFFFFFF. If you negate this value using two's complement, what is the result?
questions.explanation: 0x7FFFFFFF is 2^31 - 1 (the maximum positive 32-bit value). Negating it: flip all bits to get 0x80000000, then add 1 to get 0x80000001, which represents -(2^31 - 1).

questions.question: What is the purpose of sign extension when converting a signed 8-bit integer to a 16-bit signed integer?
choices: Replicate the sign bit to the left to preserve the value
Pad with zeros on the left to fill the extra bits
Shift the value left by 8 bits
Flip all new bits to maintain magnitude
questions.explanation: Sign extension preserves the value by replicating the sign bit (MSB) into the new higher-order bits. This maintains the numerical value when expanding a signed integer to more bits.

questions.question: In MIPS assembly, the `lb` (load byte) instruction sign-extends the loaded byte to 32 bits. If a byte containing 0xFF is loaded into register $t0, what is the resulting 32-bit value in $t0?
questions.explanation: The `lb` instruction performs sign extension: 0xFF in 8-bit two's complement is -1. The sign bit (1) is replicated to all 24 new bits, resulting in 0xFFFFFFFF.

questions.question: Consider a 4-bit two's complement number. What happens when you negate the most negative value (1000)?
choices: You get 1000 (the value remains the most negative)
questions.explanation: The most negative 4-bit value is 1000 (-8). Negating: flip to get 0111, add 1 to get 1000 again. This is an overflow case—the most negative value negates to itself in two's complement because -(-2^3) = 2^3 is outside the representable range.

questions.question: You have two 8-bit signed integers: A = 0x80 and B = 0x01. If you compute A + B in two's complement, what is the result, and is there signed overflow?
questions.explanation: 0x80 = -128 and 0x01 = 1. Adding them: -128 + 1 = -127 = 0x81. No overflow occurs because the result fits in the signed 8-bit range [-128, 127]. Signed overflow would only occur if the result exceeded this range.

questions.question: In MIPS, you need to sign-extend a 16-bit signed value in register $t1 to 32 bits. The instruction sequence uses `sll` (shift left logical) and `sra` (shift right arithmetic). What is the correct sequence?
questions.explanation: `sll $t1, $t1, 16` shifts the 16-bit value into the upper 16 bits, leaving lower bits as 0. Then `sra $t1, $t1, 16` performs arithmetic right shift, which replicates the sign bit and shifts back, achieving sign extension.

questions.question: In a 32-bit signed integer representation using two's complement, what is the range of values that can be represented?
questions.explanation: Two's complement 32-bit signed integers range from -2^31 (-2,147,483,648) to 2^31 - 1 (2,147,483,647). The negative range has one more value than the positive range due to the representation of zero.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes unsigned integer overflow?
choices: Unsigned overflow wraps around modulo 2^n, where n is the number of bits
Unsigned overflow causes a negative result
Unsigned overflow triggers a hardware exception automatically
Unsigned overflow is impossible in modern computers
questions.explanation: Unsigned overflow causes wraparound behavior due to modular arithmetic. For example, adding 1 to the maximum 8-bit unsigned value (255) results in 0. No exception is raised; it's silent wraparound.

questions.question: In 8-bit signed two's complement, what is the result of adding 127 + 1?
questions.explanation: In 8-bit signed two's complement, 127 is the maximum representable positive value. Adding 1 causes signed overflow, and the bits wrap to represent -128, the most negative value.
